rules.label: Scope
rules.text: Coaches do not diagnose or give medical nutrition therapy; symptoms go to a physician.

objective: Coaching weight management with a modest energy deficit, and recognizing when weight change is a referral question
secondaryObjectives: Recognizing when to refer to a registered dietitian nutritionist or physician: a diagnosed condition, a suspected eating disorder, pregnancy or breastfeeding needs beyond general guidance, or medications affected by diet
Setting SMART goals and choosing behavior goals over outcome goals

Her weight change on each plan and the timing of her symptoms are authored for the case: on the modest plan alone she would lose about 1 pound a week; she loses 11 pounds in four weeks because of an untreated medical cause the coach cannot name. The rate the CDC calls gradual and steady (1-2 pounds a week) and the CDC's listed symptoms are from the sources. brief.situation: You are a nutrition coach. Marisol Vega, 52 (a fictional client), wants to lose 20 pounds before her son's wedding in the fall. You set her plan today and see her again in four weeks.
handover: Coaches give general, evidence-based guidance and coach habits; diagnosing and medical nutrition therapy are outside the role.
Her intake form lists no conditions and no medications.
howItWorks: Each task takes time: choose it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes.
The screen shows the client, your read-outs and findings, the plan and the rules that apply now.
When you end the session you write the record and explain your reasoning.

safetyNote: Teaching case for exam practice; fictional client. Not medical advice.

writeup.question: For her record: what the check-in showed, what you did, and what stays within your role.

parts.label: What it showed
parts.criteria: Eleven pounds in four weeks (about 2.75 a week), faster than the plan and the CDC's 1-2 pounds a week, while eating more, with thirst, night urination, fatigue and blurred vision: symptoms the CDC lists for diabetes. A referral question, not a success.
parts.modelAnswer: She lost 11 pounds in four weeks while eating more than usual, with constant thirst, night urination, tiredness and blurry vision. That is too fast to be the plan and matches symptoms the CDC says should be checked by a doctor.

parts.label: What I did
parts.criteria: Referred her to her physician this week with notes; did not name a diagnosis or write a disease-specific meal plan; did not tighten the plan.
parts.modelAnswer: I asked her to see her physician this week and gave her my notes. I did not guess at the cause, change her plan to a 'diabetic diet' or cut her intake further.

parts.label: My role
parts.criteria: Coaching continues with general, food-first guidance and behavior goals once the physician has seen her; medical nutrition therapy, if needed, comes from her physician or a registered dietitian nutritionist.
parts.modelAnswer: I keep coaching habits within scope; anything the physician prescribes, including nutrition therapy, is theirs or a dietitian's.

referred.headline: The number was the warning
referred.body: Weight falling faster than the plan while she eats more, with thirst and night urination, is a referral question. Physician first, this week; coaching continues in your lane.

gaps.headline: Referred, with gaps
gaps.body: Check the starting plan (modest), whether you asked how she felt before celebrating, and who she was sent to (a physician first for symptoms).

lateFound.headline: A month too late
lateFound.body: Waiting another month on unexplained fast weight loss with thirst let it reach urgent care.

diagnosed.headline: Naming it is not the coach's job
diagnosed.body: Even when a pattern looks familiar, a diagnosis and a disease-specific plan belong to a physician (and a dietitian); she needed a blood test, not a diet.

noReferral.headline: Too good to be true
noReferral.body: Eleven pounds in four weeks without trying is not a coaching win. Ask how she feels, and refer.

scoring.modelReasoning: Start with a modest deficit (about 1 pound a week; the CDC calls 1-2 pounds a week gradual and steady) and behavior goals. At week 4, 11 pounds lost while eating more is faster than the plan explains; ask how she feels. Thirst, night urination, fatigue and blurred vision are symptoms the CDC says need a doctor's blood sugar test, so refer her to her physician this week with notes. Do not diagnose, write a disease-specific plan or tighten the deficit; coaching continues within scope.
